newsitem.title: USA: Clinton outraged by "cowardly" attack in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Clinton outraged by "cowardly" attack in Hebron.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday condemned an Israeli soldier's "cowardly" attempt to block a peace deal in the West Bank town of Hebron and called Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to express his condolences at the wounding of seven civilians.
Clinton took time out from his vacation to call Arafat and talk to him for about five minutes to express his sympathy.
"I told him how sorry I was. I asked him to convey my condolences to the families," the president told reporters aboard Air Force One en route to the U.S. Virgin Islands.

An off-duty Israeli soldier sprayed bullets at Arabs in a Hebron market on Wednesday, wounding seven in an attempt to sabotage a possible imminent deal on handing over Hebron to Palestinian rule and an Israeli troop withdrawal.
Clinton said he urged the parties to reach an agreement as soon as possible and told Arafat the incident illustrated how "the longer this goes on the more difficult it is."
"We need to bear down and go on," he said.

Asked why he did not telephone Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Clinton replied: "Because he didn't lose the people. I called Mr Arafat because I had to call, because they were Palestinians that were shot, if it had been Israelis that had been shot I would have called Mr Netanyahu."
Clinton expressed confidence the two leaders would go ahead with "a good faith effort" to wrap up an agreement as soon as possible.
Clinton had been hoping to hail an expected agreement on New Year's Day before flying to the Caribbean.

"The president condemns this cowardly act, which was clearly designed to make it more difficult to conclude an agreement on Israeli deployment from Hebron," White House spokeswoman, Mary Ellen Glynn said.
The United States was still hopeful Israel and the Palestinians would be able to reach an agreement on the handover of Hebron. Glynn said U.S. envoy Dennis Ross met Netanyahu as well as Arafat.
"The best answer to this action would be for the two sides to close the remaining gaps and move forward with the hard work of forging a durable peace between Israelis and Palestinians," Glynn said.
"Chairman Arafat and Prime Minister Netanyahu will have America's unwavering support as they pursue that goal," she added.

Glynn declined comment on reports from Israel that Clinton invited Netanyahu to make a visit to Washington. U.S. officials have made clear recently, however, that Clinton planned to meet Middle East leaders in the weeks and months ahead.
